list.listitem: Patients with recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) should only be tested for thrombophilias if it will affect management. B
Patients with antiphospholipid (aPL) syndrome, antithrombin III (ATIII) deficiency, protein C deficiency, and protein S deficiency are at highest risk of recurrent thromboses. B
Indefinite anticoagulation should be considered in patients at highest risk of recurrence (). C
Pregnancy confers additional risk of thromboses and consideration of prophylactic anticoagulation is warranted in birthing people with thrombophilias. C
The initial treatment of patients with acute VTE and thrombophilias does not differ from treatment of other patients. A

background.definition: Thrombophilias are hereditary or acquired defects that result in a predisposition to thrombosis.

list.listitem: Between 24% and 37% of patients with VTE have an inherited thrombophilia.
The incidence for any inherited thrombophilia in an asymptomatic control population is 10%.
In asymptomatic carriers of factor V Leiden, the annual incidence of VTE is only 0.58%.
Multiple thrombophilias may coexist. Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene are frequently found together in the Caucasian population.
Factor V Leiden: 5% to 9%; among Caucasians: 6% to 11%
Prothrombin gene mutation: 2% to 4%
Anticardiolipin antibodies: 2.7% to 7% in general obstetric population
ATIII deficiency: 0.02% to 0.2%
Protein C deficiency: 0.2% to 0.5%
Protein S deficiency: 0.08%
MTHFR (C677Tvariant): 5% to 14%
Protein C, S and ATIII deficiencies are as high as 30% in Asian populations
Factor V Leiden mutation
Prothrombin gene mutation (G20210A)

Acute medical illness including SARS-CoV2
Malignancy
Medications, particularly exogenous estrogens
Genetic mutations lead to abnormalities in the coagulation pathway resulting in increased risk of thrombosis.
Deficiencies of anticoagulant proteins (ATIII, protein C, and protein S) or excessive function of procoagulant proteins (factor V Leiden, prothrombin) may occur.
aPL syndrome can occur in the presence of lupus or alone.
Predisposition can be compounded by transient risk such as surgery, oral contraceptive (OC) use, pregnancy, infections and cancer.
Penetrance of genetic traits predisposing to thrombosis is variable and in general more severe in homozygous carriers or those with multiple mutations ().
Patients with recurrent VTE should be tested for thrombophilias if it will affect management.
Birthing people with a history of thrombosis should be offered testing in pregnancy if it will affect management.
Birthing people with recurrent early pregnancy loss or unexplained late pregnancy loss should be screened for aPL antibodies.
Consider indefinite anticoagulation for those patients at highest risk ().

Screening for thrombophilias is not recommended for asymptomatic individuals outside of pregnancy. Selective screening based on previous personal or family history of VTE is more cost-effective than universal screening.
Birthing people with a first-degree relative with known ATIII deficiency, homozygous factor V Leiden, or prothrombin gene mutation may benefit from testing.
Patients with a history of thrombosis, recurrent fetal loss, or early or severe pre-eclampsia should consider being tested if it will affect the management of future pregnancy.
The prevention of 1 death would require screening of 400,000 women prior to OC use.
Obtaining a family history of VTE is not an effective screening test for detecting thrombophilia risk before starting oral contraceptives.
Consider prophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin (UFH) prior to surgery in patients with known thrombophilic disorders (except factor V Leiden).
There is no consistent evidence that supplementation with B vitamins in patients with hyperhomocysteinemia decreases the risk of thrombotic events.
Even with a known thrombophilia, the risks of anticoagulation outweigh potential benefits in most cases for primary prevention.
Asymptomatic individuals who have persistent positive aPL do not appear to benefit from prophylactic aspirin.
Given the low annual incidence of VTE in factor V Leiden and prothrombin, prophylaxis is not recommended.
Consider indefinite anticoagulation if a patient has two or more episodes of spontaneous thrombosis, or has ATIII or aPL syndrome and one spontaneous thrombosis.

Also consider indefinite anticoagulation if a patient has one spontaneous life-threatening thrombosis (massive pulmonary embolism in the cerebral, mesenteric, or portal vein), one spontaneous thrombosis at an unusual site, or one spontaneous thrombosis in presence of multiple thrombophilic genetic defects.
Prothrombotic abnormalities do not appear to play an important role in recurrent VTE risk, and clinical factors are probably more important.
Refer to the international consensus statement for diagnostic criteria for aPL syndrome.
Diagnosis requires the persistent presence of an aPL antibody (at least 12 weeks apart) and at least one of the following: venous or arterial thrombosis, recurrent fetal loss, or thrombocytopenia.
Thrombophilias are asymptomatic unless they lead to VTE.
In half of patients with hereditary thrombophilia, the initial thrombotic event occurs in the presence of an additional risk factor (ie, pregnancy, OCP use, or surgery).
See separate chapters on deep vein thrombosis, arterial embolism, and pulmonary embolism for a more detailed discussion of their clinical diagnoses.
Suspect thrombophilias in birthing people with early or severe pre-eclampsia, unexplained fetal loss or stillbirth, intrauterine growth retardation, or placental abruption.
Whether testing patients for thrombophilia's who present with recurrent VTE improves outcomes is is not clear.
A Cochrane review concluded that there are no RCTs on the benefit(s) of tests for thrombophilia on the risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism.
The NICE guideline specifies that the only clear indication for thrombophilia testing is when consideration is being given to discontinuing anticoagulant therapy after an unprovoked VTE event.

Guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends testing for antiphopholipid antibodies for the following situations: >1 clinical episode of arterial or venous thrombosis. >1 unexplained death of fetuses older than 9 weeks gestation. >1 premature birth due to pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or placental insufficiency. >3 unexplained pregnancy losses before gestation age week 10.
If testing is pursued, defer testing for protein C, protein S, and ATIII deficiency in patients with acute thrombosis, on anticoagulation, or during pregnancy.
Test results for ATIII deficiency, protein C, and protein S may be falsely lowered in the setting of extensive clotting, warfarin use, or heparin administration.
Individuals with a strong family history of thrombophilias are more likely to have multiple inherited risk factors.
Consider testing for aPL antibodies in patients with unexplained arterial thrombosis.
DNA testing for factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A mutation is considered reliable in pregnancy.
Patients with retinal vascular occlusion are not more likely to have a thrombophilia based on a meta-analysis of 29 studies, so routine testing is not indicated for these patients.

Among 3334 consecutive patients admitted with COVID-19 between March 1 and April 19, 2020, pulmonary emboli occurred in 6.2% of the patients in the ICU and 2.2% on the ward; deep vein thrombosis in 9.4% ICU and 2.0% ward patients; strokes 3.7% and 0.9%; myocardial infarction 13.9% and 7.3% respectively.

The adjusted Global Anti-Phospholipid Syndrome Score (aGAPSS) is higher in patients who go on to have a thrombotic event or pregnancy complication. A score greater than 13 has 56% positive predictive value and 74% negative predictive value. An online version of the calculator can be found here.
Treatment of initial VTE in patients with thrombophilias does not differ from those without thrombophilias.
See chapters on deep vein thrombosis, arterial embolism, and pulmonary embolism for specifics of treatment.
Patients with ATIII deficiency may be resistant to heparin therapy and require large doses. Severe cases may require the use of antithrombin concentrate.

Patients with protein C deficiency are at risk for warfarin-induced skin necrosis. For patients with known protein C deficiency, start oral anticoagulation once fully heparinized at a low dose and increase slowly.
High-intensity anticoagulation is not better than standard anticoagulation in patients with aPL syndrome.
Several thrombophilias have been associated with early or severe preeclampsia, unexplained fetal loss or stillbirth, and placental abruption.

A Cochrane review concluded that for women at high risk for preeclampsia or miscarriage, low molecular weight heparin reduces the likelihood of pre-eclampsia (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43-0.90), small for gestational age (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.44-0.85) and perinatal death (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.25-0.94). It is more effective when started before 16 weeks and when combined with low dose aspirin.
VTE treatment should be 3 months minimum in those with known thrombophilia.
For birthing people with acute VTE, therapy should be continued during the pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum for a minimum duration of 6 months.
Patients with aPL antibody syndrome are generally recommended to have lifelong anticoagulation therapy because of high recurrence risk.
Birthing people with known thrombophilia should be managed by a physician experienced in managing anticoagulation during pregnancy.
For warfarin-induced skin necrosis and heterozygous protein C deficiency, administer fresh frozen plasma or protein C concentrate until the patient is stable on oral anticoagulation.
Patients with ATIII deficiency, protein C deficiency, or protein S deficiency have 7- to 8-fold lifetime increase in risk of VTE.
Patients with factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutation have a low overall incidence of VTE, although they are the most frequently encountered thrombophilias in Caucasians.
aPL: The recurrence rate of thrombosis in patients with untreated aPL syndrome is 25%. Among those with aPL antibodies, 0.5% to 2% will develop thromboses each year.

Thrombophilia and pregnancy: In birthing people with recurrent fetal loss and no prior thrombosis, the risk of thrombosis is approximately 10% per year. Conversely, women with prior VTE have a recurrence rate of 7.5% to 12% during pregnancy.

Factor V Leiden: A large Danish study found that the hazard ratio for VTE was 2.2 for heterozygotes and 7.0 for homozygotes for Factor V Leiden. Risk was increased in patients who also had non-O ABO blood type. The risk of myocardial infarction was not increased. Heterozygosity for factor V Leiden does not increase overall mortality rate.
Prothrombin G20210A: A large Danish study found that the hazard ratio for VTE was 1.5 for heterozygotes and 11 for homozygotes. Risk was increased in patients who also had non-O ABO blood type.

Protein S and C deficiency: The lifetime risk ratio of VTE is 8.5 for patients with protein S deficiency, 8.1 for those with antithrombin, 7.3 for protein C deficiency, and 2.2 for factor V Leiden (both heterozygotes and homozygotes) compared with control patients.
It is important to remember that the strongest risk for recurrent VTE is prior VTE itself, not the thrombophilia.

Thrombophilia disorders are present in 14% of patients who experience a myocardial infarction in the absence of obstructed coronary arteries.Patients with non O blood type have increased risk for recurrent VTE after first unprovoked VTE (HR 1.98)
Reconsider long-term anticoagulation in those with thrombophilias on the basis of the emergence or disappearance of additional risk factors.
Overall risk for VTE is highest for those with protein C, protein S, or ATIII deficiencies ().

A systematic review of 89 studies with 30,254 persons found that the risk of pregnancy loss was significantly higher among birthing people with Factor V Leiden (OR 2.4), prothrombin gene mutation (OR 2.1), or protein S deficiency.
Consider screening birthing people with prior VTE or family history of first degree relative with history of high risk thrombophilia.
Low-dose aspirin plus heparin was found to be the most beneficial in preventing pregnancy loss in thrombophilic birthing people.

Risk of VTE is highest in pregnancy for birthing people with artificial heart valves, ATIII deficiency, aPL antibody syndrome, history of rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation, homozygous carriers of factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutation, and those using chronic anticoagulation for recurrent VTE.

ACCP guidelines recommend that birthing people with a high-risk thrombophilia and single prior VTE should receive prophylactic or intermediate-dose heparin during pregnancy in addition to postpartum anticoagulation.

However, a RCT of 292 pregnant women with thrombophilia who were at increased risk of VTE concluded that there was no effect of antepartum dalteparin (5000 Uunits once daily up to 20 weeks gestation, and twice daily from 20 to 37 weeks) on the occurrance of VTE, pregnancy loss or placenta-mediated pregnancy complications. There was an increased risk of minor bleeding.
Birthing people with multiple prior VTEs and not using long-term anticoagulation should receive prophylactic, intermediate-dose, or adjusted-dose heparin throughout pregnancy.

Birthing people with a thrombophilia and no prior VTE may be followed up clinically or treated with prophylactic heparin during pregnancy and anticoagulation in the postpartum period. Unfortunately, good clinical trials are lacking and many recommendations are based on limited observational studies or expert opinion.

Women who test positive for aPL antibody should be treated during pregnancy with prophylactic or intermediate-dose heparin and low-dose aspirin. A systematic review found that heparin plus aspirin was more effective than aspirin alone among women with aPL syndrome. Women with antithrombin deficiency and no prior VTE should receive prophylaxis during the antepartum and postpartum period.
Warfarin should be avoided in pregnancy (except in the case of mechanical heart valves) because of teratogenic effects on the fetus.

Prophylaxis in pregnancy refers to a fixed dose of anticoagulant 1 or 2 times daily (UFH 5000 units subcutaneously every 12 hours or enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously every 24 hours). Intermediate dose is fixed twice-daily dosing at higher doses than prophylaxis (UFH every 12 hours for anti-Xa level 0.1-0.3 or enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously every 12 hours). Adjusted-dose prophylaxis refers to 2 or 3 times daily dosing to achieve traditional therapeutic effects (UFH every 12 hours to target aPTT 1.5-2.5 times normal or enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours).
Infants born to mothers with aPL antibodies may be at increased risk of arterial thromboses.
Warfarin and heparins are considered compatible with breastfeeding.
